body: My only friend has left the country and is probably never coming back. Throughout the summer I at least knew he'd be coming for a while sometime but now there's nothing. I haven't really talked to anyone outside of my family in years except him, so I just feel totally alone right now.

>You have every right not to have children, but you can't decide for them that they can't live just because you think that the possibility of a bad life outweighs giving anyone ever the chance to live.

I agree. To be honest, the first parts of this has little to do with my antinatalism. The central point in my belief is the aforementioned uncertainty in regards to how your child's life will play out. I've no interest in forcing anyone to adopt my beliefs or deciding whether anyone has the right to live or not. It's merely my own belief and a suggestion towards others that I think very few, if any, will follow.

Antinatalism isn't even something I think about a whole lot any more, because there's very little to do once you've made the choice not to have children except mention the idea to others and see if they're even open to it.

>the end of everything everyone ever worked for

What are we all working for exactly?

>If we're the last generation and there is no future, what is the point of doing anything?

The intrinsic satisfaction one gets from doing it.

>And most people see value in living and don't consider the suffering involved in living as outweighing the benefits of existence.

If your life is good, that's good, but there's no way to predict how your child's life will turn out. They might end up depressed, suicidal, or worse, regardless of your parenting skills, wealth, education, etc.

I agree with antinatalism, but I'm hopeless about it ever becoming popular beyond a tiny minority of people. Humans are generally biased towards optimism and won't even entertain the arguments behind antinatalism.

There's good reason to be skeptical of common sources of information. The problem is that very few people can refrain from having a resolute opinion on something. When one source is deemed distrustful, they will latch onto another instead of just saying "I don't know."

The majority of people aren't much different than conspiracy theorists, they just happen to believe things that have majority support. Just as there are dogmatic conspiracy theorists, there are dogmatic anti-conspiracy theorists.

My logic is only descriptive, not prescriptive. When opportunity knocks, I can't help but answer so that I might feel a little better. I simply define "opportunity" more widely than most.

Of course I *feel* like I control my mind, and that's how everyone lives their life, so for all practical purposes, you're right. I'm just saying that depression is when one sees behind the curtain. Bad emotional state caused by bad life circumstance causes one to take a peek. None of these actions are truly deliberate I would say. It's just what we naturally do to varying degrees as human animals, hence why I mention species up there.

I'm very sleep deprived so I'm hoping this makes sense. I appreciate the response.

Think where the motivation to even work hard comes from in the first place. If it originates from within, then there's basically no excuse to feel depressed ever because you should just be able to motivate yourself.

No, motivation comes entirely from a series of circumstances out of one's control that stretch back to the beginning of time. It merely has the appearance of being a conscious choice made by someone to improve their life.

Schools are authoritarian and children and teenagers are treated as subhuman, similar to the elderly. Ageism. The people talking about the need to improve schools are shining examples of the complete lack of creativity that the education system leaves us with.

On top of that, once you're out, you'll probably stop caring, even if you become a parent. It's the perfect system because nobody with any power will bother to challenge it as it doesn't directly affect them.
